title: Episode 322: William III & Mary II: The Bill of Rights, Glencoe, and the Constitutional Monarchy
description:
The monumental, dual reign of King William III and Queen Mary II, the architects of modern British constitutional democracy. Invited by English peers to depose James II in 1688, Dutch Stadtholder William of Orange and his devoted English wife Mary were crowned as equal joint monarchs in 1689. Accepting the revolutionary Bill of Rights, they permanently subordinated the Crown to Parliament, guaranteeing free elections, free speech in Parliament, and the rule of law. While William fought across European battlefields against Louis XIV and navigated the dark shame of the Massacre of Glencoe, Mary governed England with grace and wisdom until smallpox claimed her at thirty-two. Discover the sovereigns who forged the modern constitutional monarchy.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, our Kings and Queens of England series examines the unique joint monarchy that reshaped the destiny of Britain: the Dutch prince and English princess who established the Bill of Rights and constitutional liberty: King William III and Queen Mary II. Here is George with the grand story of the dual monarchs.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE DUTCH MATCH: WESTMINSTER TO THE HAGUE: 1662 TO 1688
Born in April 1662 at St. James's Palace, Mary Stuart was the eldest daughter of James, Duke of York, and Anne Hyde. Beautiful, tall, and devoutly Protestant, fifteen-year-old Mary was horrified in 1677 when her uncle Charles II commanded her to marry her Dutch cousin, William, Prince of Orange—weeping uncontrollably for an entire afternoon. William was twelve years her senior, slight of build, asthmatic, serious, and obsessed with the defense of the Dutch Republic against the imperial aggression of Louis XIV's France. Yet over twelve years in Holland, at their palaces of Huis ten Bosch and Het Loo, Mary's gentle grace and steadfast loyalty won William's profound respect and devoted affection. Mary immersed herself in Dutch culture, gardening, and collecting blue-and-white Delft porcelain, while William came to rely completely on her emotional support as he forged continental coalitions to preserve European Protestant liberties. William of Orange was born a posthumous child in November 1650, his father William II having died of smallpox eight days before his birth. Raised in the shadow of the anti-Orangist Dutch oligarchs, twenty-one-year-old William became Stadtholder during the 'Disaster Year' of 1672, when Louis XIV invaded the Netherlands. In a desperate act of military genius, William ordered the sea dykes breached, flooding the Dutch countryside to halt the French armies outside Amsterdam, swearing he would die in the last ditch before surrendering Dutch liberty. His marriage to Mary Stuart was a brilliant geopolitical alliance, uniting the House of Orange with the English royal succession to form an unbreakable Protestant barrier against French domination.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE JOINT CROWN AND THE BILL OF RIGHTS: 1689
Following the flight of James II in the Glorious Revolution, the Convention Parliament faced an unprecedented constitutional crisis: who held the crown? Tories argued that Mary should reign alone as legitimate hereditary queen, with William as mere prince consort. William coldly informed the lords that he would not be his wife's gentleman usher, threatening to take his army back to Holland if he was not made king for life. Mary display loyalty to her husband, insisting she would not reign without William. In February 1689, in the Banqueting House at Whitehall, Parliament presented the Declaration of Rights to William and Mary, offering them the crown as joint sovereigns with equal royal dignity—the only joint monarchy in British history. Codified into law as the Bill of Rights in December 1689, this historic statute permanently ended absolute monarchy in Britain: it banned the royal dispensing power, forbade standing armies in peacetime without parliamentary consent, established free parliamentary elections, guaranteed freedom of speech in debates, and barred any Roman Catholic from ever inheriting the British throne. The Declaration of Rights presented to William and Mary in the Banqueting House on February 13, 1689, was the foundational constitutional charter of the modern English-speaking world. It explicitly established that the King could not suspend laws, levy taxes, or maintain a standing army without the consent of Parliament. By accepting the crown on these terms, William and Mary transformed the British monarchy from an autocracy based on Divine Right into a constitutional monarchy based on a legal contract between sovereign and people, inspiring the American Declaration of Independence and Constitution a century later.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE SCOTTISH HIGHLANDS: KILLIECRANKIE AND THE MASSACRE OF GLENCOE: 1689 TO 1692
While England embraced the new regime, Scotland erupted in Jacobite insurrection. In July 1689, John Graham of Claverhouse, 'Bonnie Dundee', rallied the Highland clans for James II, routing Williamite forces at the Pass of Killiecrankie before being killed in the moment of victory. To pacify the Highlands, William's government offered a general pardon to all clan chiefs who took an oath of allegiance before a magistrate by January 1, 1692. Alasdair MacIain, chief of the MacDonalds of Glencoe, was delayed by severe blizzards, taking the oath six days late. Seizing the pretext to eradicate what he viewed as a clan of thieves, the Secretary of State for Scotland, John Dalrymple, Master of Stair, procured William's signature on a ruthless royal order. In February 1692, two companies of the Earl of Argyll's regiment, commanded by Robert Campbell of Glenlyon, quartered with the MacDonalds for twelve days under the sacred laws of Highland hospitality. At five in the morning on February 13, in the middle of a blinding snowstorm, the soldiers turned upon their sleeping hosts: thirty-eight MacDonalds were butchered in their beds, and forty women and children perished in the freezing mountains. The Massacre of Glencoe stained William's reputation forever. The Massacre of Glencoe remains one of the darkest crimes in Scottish history: Captain Robert Campbell of Glenlyon and his troops had lived among the MacDonalds for nearly two weeks, sharing their food, drinking their usquebaugh, and playing cards with their hosts. On the night of February 13, 1692, the order was carried out with chilling brutality: old Chief MacIain was shot through the back as he rose from his bed to order morning wine for his guests. Though William claimed he had signed the order 'in the hurry of many affairs' without reading the details, the Scottish Parliament conducted an inquiry in 1695 that condemned the massacre as murder under trust, staining William's memory across the Highlands for generations.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE GOVERNED REALM: QUEEN MARY AT WHITEHALL: 1690 TO 1694
Because William spent each spring and summer on the continent commanding Allied armies against France in the Nine Years' War, governance of England fell entirely upon Queen Mary. Operating with a council of nine ministers—whom she privately described as squabbling, self-interested intriguers—Mary demonstrated extraordinary administrative competence, political firmness, and personal courage. When the French fleet defeated the Anglo-Dutch navy at Beachy Head in 1690 and panic swept the capital, Mary calmly inspected the militia, fortified the coast, and rallied London merchants to loan money to the Crown. Concurrently, Mary was an architectural patron of transcendent vision: together with Christopher Wren, she transformed Hampton Court Palace into an English Versailles with its magnificent red-brick and Portland stone Baroque facade, and founded the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich to care for disabled naval veterans, earning the deep and abiding adoration of the English people. Queen Mary's solo regencies while William campaigned abroad demonstrated remarkable political acumen and regal dignity. Her council of nine ministers, divided between Whigs and Tories, constantly plotted behind her back; yet Mary managed them with calm, unyielding authority. Her passion for architecture and design revolutionized English taste: she commissioned Sir Christopher Wren to build the Baroque East Wing of Hampton Court Palace and the Royal Hospital for Seamen at Greenwich, popularized Delftware blue-and-white ceramics, and introduced English society to the ritual of drinking tea in delicate porcelain cups.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE TRAGIC SMALLPOX: THE DEATH OF QUEEN MARY: DECEMBER 1694
In December 1694, catastrophe struck the royal household: thirty-two-year-old Queen Mary contracted smallpox at Kensington Palace. Recognizing that her illness was fatal, Mary spent her final conscious hours burning her private correspondence to protect her friends, refusing to allow anyone who had not previously survived smallpox to enter her bedchamber. William, notoriously cold and unemotional to the outside world, broke down in hysterical, inconsolable grief: he collapsed fainting beside her bed, ordering a camp bed placed in her room so he would never leave her side, sobbing to Bishop Gilbert Burnet that from being the happiest man on earth, he was now the most miserable creature. On December 28, 1694, Queen Mary II died. The entire nation fell into profound mourning. On a freezing, snow-swept March day, Mary was given the grandest royal funeral in British history at Westminster Abbey, accompanied by the haunting, transcendent funeral music composed by Henry Purcell, with all members of Parliament marching in black mourning robes. The grief of King William upon Mary's death in December 1694 stunned courtiers who had viewed the Dutch prince as an unfeeling, phlegmatic soldier. For weeks after her passing, William was incapacitated by fainting spells, refusing to attend to state papers or council meetings, sleeping on a camp bed in her former apartments. Henry Purcell's transcendent Funeral Sentences and March for Queen Mary, with its somber muted brass and echoing kettle drums, captured the profound national sorrow for a beloved queen who had embodied the gentle, reconciling conscience of the Glorious Revolution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BANK OF ENGLAND, THE DARIEN DISASTER, AND THE ACT OF SETTLEMENT: 1694 TO 1701
Governing alone, William faced immense financial and constitutional challenges. To finance his colossal European war against Louis XIV, William's government founded the Bank of England in 1694 and established the National Debt, revolutionizing world public finance by enabling the state to borrow immense capital at low interest rates, laying the economic foundation for the British Empire. Concurrently, Scotland was ruined by the Darien Disaster—a catastrophic attempt to establish a Scottish trading colony on the Isthmus of Panama, which collapsed from disease and Spanish attacks, bankrupting a quarter of all Scottish capital, convincing William that a complete legislative union between England and Scotland was an urgent necessity. In 1701, following the death of Princess Anne's only surviving child, Parliament passed the historic Act of Settlement: bypassing dozens of Catholic claimants, it decreed that the crown would pass to the Protestant Electress Sophia of Hanover and her heirs, permanently securing the Protestant succession. The creation of the Bank of England in 1694 by Scottish merchant William Paterson revolutionized global finance: in exchange for a loan of one point two million pounds to the government to fund the war with France, the bank was granted a royal charter to issue bank notes, inventing modern paper currency and government bonds. Concurrently, the catastrophic collapse of the Scottish Darien scheme in the jungles of Panama created an existential economic crisis in Edinburgh, paving the way for the historic 1707 Act of Union that united England and Scotland into the Kingdom of Great Britain.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE SORREL MOLEHILL AND THE PASSING OF THE KING: 1702
In early 1702, William stood on the brink of his greatest military endeavor: having negotiated the Grand Alliance between England, the Dutch Republic, and the Holy Roman Empire, he prepared to lead Allied forces in the War of the Spanish Succession to prevent France from dominating Europe. But destiny intervened in Hampton Court Park on February 21, 1702. While riding his favorite horse, Sorrel, the horse stumbled upon an underground molehill; fifty-one-year-old William was thrown violently, breaking his collarbone. Weakened by chronic asthma and pneumonia, William was taken to Kensington Palace. On March 8, 1702, King William III died peacefully, clutching a black silk ribbon tied around his wrist containing a lock of Mary's hair and her wedding ring. Jacobite rebels raised secret toasts to 'the little gentleman in black velvet'—the mole that had unseated the king. William was buried beside Mary in Westminster Abbey. Through unyielding courage and constitutional wisdom, the Dutch prince had defended European Protestantism, established the Bill of Rights, and cemented the enduring foundation of modern parliamentary democracy. William's fatal fall from his horse Sorrel in Hampton Court Park in February 1702 was caused by a mole burrowing beneath the turf. The King suffered a fractured collarbone; weakened by pleurisy and chronic asthma, he died at Kensington Palace on March 8, 1702. On his deathbed, William gave his blessing to his sister-in-law, Queen Anne, and urged his counselors to complete the Grand Alliance against France. Buried beside Mary in Westminster Abbey, William of Orange left behind an indelible legacy: he had contained the imperial ambition of Louis XIV, forged the financial power of the City of London, and secured the enduring triumph of parliamentary democracy.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Thank you for joining us for this episode of Most Fascinating Stories. If you enjoyed this chapter of William III & Mary II: The Bill of Rights, Glencoe, and the Constitutional Monarchy, subscribe to the show, share it with a fellow history lover, and tune in next Tuesday for our next journey into history's most extraordinary events. Until next time, I'm Rebecca.
